assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reaching 10^-18 fractional uncertainty are a textbook case of a measurement advance opening new physics: redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre level, dark-matter and fundamental-constant searches. The magic-wavelength lattice idea and its demonstration are original, and the clarity of the performance metrics (stability, systematic uncertainty) is exactly what an experimentalist wants.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and built the first Sr lattice clock; Ye's JILA group pushed the Sr clock to the 10^-18 regime and the many-body/spin-exchange understanding. A two-person prize is clean. Other groups (Lemke/Ludlow at NIST, Hinkley, PTB, Yb clocks) contributed and may be argued for, and ion clocks (Wineland/Hall lineage) are partly recognised already.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many laboratories worldwide with agreement at the 10^-18 level; the technology is stable and the field is moving toward a redefinition of the SI second. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Allocation versus other optical-clock groups (Yb lattice clocks, Al+ ion clocks) is not settled in the supplied credit.
I recall, but have not verified here, details of the individual priority claims for the magic-wavelength concept.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument: gravimeters, gyroscopes, measurements of G and of the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. This is the kind of method that expands what can be measured, and it has already produced devices.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theoretical framework, Pritchard's early atom-optics and interferometer demonstrations (with Mlynek, Chu and Kasevich also central to the early work), and Kasevich's inertial-sensing results make a plausible three-person set. Steven Chu was already recognised for laser cooling, and the Mlynek and Kasevich-Chu priority question is not resolved by the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Strong replication and a mature set of applications (commercial gravimeters, long-baseline fountains, geodesy). Fundamental-physics reach (e.g. dark-energy and equivalence-principle tests) is still developing, but the method itself is established.
uncertainties: Attribution among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and Mlynek is contested.
Whether the most important results are yet to come (large-scale space or km-scale instruments) is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry, from Caves's proposal to Kimble's early squeezing experiments and routine use in gravitational-wave detectors. It is a clear, general quantum-metrology advance with direct payoff in the most sensitive instruments ever built.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the decisive theoretical proposal, Kimble the first experimental squeezed-state generation in the 1980s, and Schnabel the long-term development of audio-band squeezing for GEO600 and LIGO. Mavalvala and others (Slusher, Wu) are credited too, and four names exceed the three-person limit, so the choice is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Operationally mature: squeezed vacuum is installed in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 and improves detection rates. Interpretation is stable, and independent groups have confirmed the techniques.
uncertainties: Slusher's first squeezing observation and Mavalvala's LIGO implementation are not in my proposed set, which is an allocation weakness.
Part of the downstream impact overlaps with the 2017 prize for LIGO.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration correction broke a nearly century-old limit in electron lens design and brought routine sub-ångström imaging and single-atom spectroscopy in TEM and STEM. It is an instrument invention with huge enabling impact across materials physics and nanoscience, and the idea is conceptually clear (multipole correctors).
assessment.attribution: Rose provided the corrector theory, Haider built the first working TEM corrector (with Rose and Uhlemann), and Krivanek realised the STEM corrector. Knut Urban, who applied it to materials, is not in the supplied credited names, and that is a gap in a fair prize configuration. A three-person prize from these names is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: commercial adoption, thousands of results, independent confirmation, and earlier recognition (Kavli Prize 2020, Wolf Prize). Electron-microscopy recognition in physics has precedent (Ruska 1986).
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as physics rather than instrumentation or chemistry.
Absence of Urban from the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and control of single NV centres opened room-temperature quantum sensing at the nanoscale: magnetometry, thermometry, NMR of tiny volumes and biological applications. It is a measurement platform with real impact beyond physics, and I would weigh coherence times and sensitivity numbers carefully.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup (with Gruber, 1997) first detected single NV centres optically, Lukin and Walsworth drove the nanoscale-sensing demonstrations and many-body use. Credit is spread over several groups (Awschalom, Hanson, Jelezko, Hollenberg, Yacoby, Budker), so a three-name configuration is difficult to defend.
assessment.maturity: Replication is broad and the field is expanding, but sensor performance and sensitivity relative to existing techniques still evolve, and commercial maturity is limited. Possibly slightly premature.
uncertainties: Distribution of credit among the many groups, including Jelezko and Awschalom, is unclear.
Competing sensing platforms may limit long-term dominance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models with controlled parameters, such as the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and quantum gas microscopy, giving a new way to observe many-body physics. It is a clear conceptual and experimental advance with a large community.
assessment.attribution: Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger delivered the key experimental breakthroughs (Mott transition, fermionic lattices, microscopy), while Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac supplied the foundational proposals. An experimental trio is plausible but sidelines the theory, and five credited names reveal the difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many laboratories and mature as a platform; the open question is whether it has yet delivered a decisive result unreachable by other means, so the field's strongest payoff may still be ahead.
uncertainties: Balance between theory (Zoller, Cirac, Jaksch) and experiment is unresolved.
Unclear whether simulation advantage over classical methods is convincingly established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 completed the Standard Model and was among the great experimental achievements: detectors, triggers, analysis and the careful separation of signal from background. The measurement was clear and has been repeatedly confirmed.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize went to the theorists, so the experimental side has been left open. A fair configuration is difficult given collaborations of thousands; the founders and leaders of ATLAS (Jenni) and CMS (Della Negra, Virdee) are the natural choices, while Gianotti, as ATLAS spokesperson at the time of discovery, is a strong alternative. The Nobel statutes' limit of three and the two-experiment structure make the allocation contested.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: both experiments independently observed it, couplings have been measured, and the interpretation is stable. The committee has long accepted that the experimental credit is a problem rather than a maturity concern.
uncertainties: Allocation among ATLAS and CMS leadership and whether a collaboration-level prize is acceptable.
Whether leaders of detector construction or physics analysis best represent the decisive contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Ti:sapphire laser and passive mode-locking made femtosecond pulses practical and compact and underpin ultrafast spectroscopy, frequency combs and attosecond science. It is a broad enabling tool, with clear originality in gain medium and in Kerr-lens and SESAM mode-locking.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed Ti:sapphire, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking, and Keller invented the SESAM. The three roles are distinct and a three-person prize looks plausible, though the Kerr-lens discovery history (Spence, Kean, Sibbett) and the 2018 chirped-pulse prize both complicate matters.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and ubiquitous in laboratories and industry. The remaining question is whether the committee considers this instrumentation already adequately covered by the 1999, 2005, 2018 and 2023 prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with previous ultrafast and laser prizes may reduce novelty in the committee's view.
Priority history of Kerr-lens mode-locking is partly uncertain in my recollection.
